observation_summary: The DateUtils.truncate method incorrectly handles Daylight Saving Time (DST) transitions because the underlying Calendar.set() calls trigger side effects (resetting DST_OFFSET) even when the field value remains unchanged.
hypothesis: The original implementation relied on Calendar.set() to perform truncation, which is side-effect prone during DST transitions. The fix replaces this with a manual calculation of the time in milliseconds, avoiding unnecessary Calendar.set() calls that cause the DST_OFFSET to be reset incorrectly.
prediction: The code will perform manual arithmetic on the time value (in milliseconds) to truncate fields, only updating the Calendar object when a change is actually required, thus avoiding the side effects of Calendar.set().
experiment_rationale: The diff shows a complete rewrite of the truncation logic, moving from relying on Calendar.set() to manual long-based arithmetic for milliseconds, seconds, and minutes, and adding a conditional check before updating the Calendar object.
reasoning_summary: The fix is an algorithmic rewrite of the truncation procedure. It replaces a reliance on a library method (Calendar.set) that had unintended side effects with a manual computational strategy that calculates the truncated time directly. This is a classic procedural correction to an incorrect computational strategy.
evidence_used: The diff shows the removal of reliance on Calendar.set() for truncation and the introduction of manual time arithmetic.
The bug report notes that Calendar.set() resets DST_OFFSET even when the value is unchanged.
The fix introduces a manual calculation of time and only updates the Calendar object if the time has actually changed.

alternative_types.why_not_primary: While the fix adds a check (if (offset != 0)), the primary mechanism of the fix is the complete replacement of the truncation logic with a new computational strategy.
The fix is not about setting a wrong value, but about changing the entire procedure used to calculate the truncated date.
